source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει·
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen by the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. For Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, also called Plistonicus, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he is hostile towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and has even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king in the place of Argive Inachus, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemy of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. This Ptolemy was a priest, and in three whole books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and according to him, during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their journey out of Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles; and of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger; and the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine; and this one is also said to be autochthonous. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are two generations younger. And going back to the time of the Trojan War from Inachus, twenty or a few more generations are counted, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the Assyrian things are much older than the Greek, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the movement of Moses out of Egypt, during the reign of Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, occurred. And in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there was the flood of Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born;
pass_b_english: We will address a little later the question of whether the philosophers' doctrines were seen by the Hebrews; first, as is fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown unmistakably that the philosophy of the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has treated these matters precisely in his *Address to the Greeks*, and Cassian has also done so in the first of his *Exegetical* works; nevertheless, this memorandum requires us to run through the statements made in the relevant place. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian History*—though he is hostile toward the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and has even composed a book against the Jews—mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and adduces Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's words are these: "Amosis, having become king in the time of the Argive Inachus, dug up Avaris," as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest, and he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books; according to him, during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of Greek histories are the Argolic—that is, those reckoned from Inachus—as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Of these, the Attic chronicles, which begin with Cecrops the two‑natured and autochthonous, are forty generations younger, as Tatian says word for word; the Arcadian chronicles, which begin with Pelasgus—who is also said to be autochthonous—are nine generations younger; and the Phthiotic chronicles, which begin with Deucalion, are two generations younger still. Reckoning back to the time of the Trojan War from Inachus, twenty or a few more generations are counted, amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years. But if Assyrian history is older than Greek by many years, as Ctesias says, it will appear that the movement of Moses out of Egypt, in the reign of Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, occurred in the 402nd year of the Assyrian empire and in the 32nd year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, the flood of Ogyges took place and the kingdom in Sicyon began—first Aegialeus, then Europs, then Telchin—and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and historical citations. Pass A preserves the sense of all clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that remains faithful to the Greek syntax and meaning. The distinction between the different Greek lineages (Argolic, Attic, Arcadian, Phthiotic) and their generational offsets is correctly rendered in both. The specific years mentioned (402nd and 32nd) are correctly translated from the Greek 'δεύτερῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ' and 'δεύτερῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ'.
